blocks.text: You already know how to grab specific rows with .loc and .iloc when you know exactly which row you want. But most of the time you do not know the exact row, you know a CONDITION. You want every order over five hundred dollars, every user who signed up last month, every sensor reading above a threshold. That is filtering, and it is one of the most used skills in all of pandas. If you already worked through boolean masking on NumPy arrays, you are going to recognize almost everything here immediately, because a DataFrame filter is the exact same idea applied to a table instead of a plain array.

blocks.alt: A boolean condition on a DataFrame producing only the matching rows
blocks.caption: One condition, one line, and you have exactly the rows you wanted.

blocks.text: 1. Introduction

Filtering a DataFrame means keeping only the rows that satisfy some condition. Pandas gives you several ways to do this, from a simple comparison to a full query string, and picking the right one depends mostly on how complex your condition is and how readable you want the result to be.
2. Boolean Condition Filtering
The most basic form is writing a comparison on a column, which gives you a boolean Series, then using that boolean Series to index the DataFrame.

This is exactly the same mental model as NumPy boolean masking, just scoped to rows of a table instead of elements of an array. df["total"] > 500 produces a Series of True and False, one per row, and df[...] keeps only the rows where that Series is True.
2.1 Combining Multiple Conditions

To combine two or more conditions, use the bitwise operators & for and, | for or, never Python's own and/or. Each individual condition needs its own parentheses, since Python's operator precedence would otherwise evaluate & before the comparisons themselves and break the expression.

blocks.alt: Two conditions each wrapped in parentheses before being combined with the bitwise and operator
blocks.caption: Each side of the and needs its own parentheses, every time.

blocks.alt: Dropping the parentheses around each condition causing a TypeError
blocks.caption: This is the single most common syntax mistake in pandas filtering.

blocks.title: Parentheses are not optional
blocks.content: Without parentheses around each condition, Python tries to evaluate df.a > 5 & df.b as one expression before comparing to 10, which either raises an error or silently does the wrong thing. Wrap every individual condition in parens whenever you combine them.

blocks.text: 2.2 Why and/or Do Not Work Here

Python's built in and/or expect a single True or False value on each side. A condition like df.a > 5 is not a single value, it is a whole Series of True/False values, one per row. Python has no idea how to collapse a Series down to one true or false answer, so it raises an error instead of guessing.

blocks.alt: Python's and operator failing on a Series with an ambiguous truth value error
blocks.caption: This is the exact same root cause as the and/or gotcha from NumPy boolean masking.

code.content:
df[df.a > 5 and df.b < 10]
# ValueError: The truth value of a Series is ambiguous.

blocks.text: 3. A More Readable Alternative: query()

For anything more complex than a couple of conditions, .query() often reads more like plain English. You write your condition as a string, reference column names directly without repeating df[...] everywhere, and you can use plain and/or inside the string instead of &/|.

blocks.alt: The same filter expressed through query, reading closer to plain English
blocks.caption: Same result, noticeably easier to read once you have more than two conditions.

blocks.title: query strings use plain and/or
blocks.content: Inside a query string, and/or work exactly as you would expect, because pandas parses the string itself rather than relying on Python's own boolean operators on a Series.

blocks.text: 4. Membership Filtering with isin
When you want to keep rows where a column matches ANY value from a list, .isin() is cleaner than chaining a pile of == comparisons with |.

blocks.alt: isin checking a column against a list of acceptable values
blocks.caption: One call instead of stacking several == comparisons with or.

blocks.text: 5. Negating a Condition with ~
The tilde operator flips a boolean condition, letting you express what you want to exclude instead of what you want to keep.

blocks.alt: The tilde operator negating an isin condition to exclude matching rows instead of keep them
blocks.caption: Same isin check, opposite outcome.

blocks.alt: Keeping only rows with a specific status versus excluding rows with a specific status
blocks.caption: Two mirror image patterns you will use constantly: keep only versus drop only.

blocks.text: 6. A Preview of String Based Filtering
You can also filter on text content using the .str accessor, which you will cover in full depth in a dedicated lesson later in this module. For now, just know it exists.

blocks.alt: str.contains filtering rows where a text column contains a given substring
blocks.caption: A small preview of what the string operations lesson covers in depth.

blocks.text: 7. Worked Example: High Value Orders From Specific Regions

Say you have an orders DataFrame and you want to find every order over five hundred dollars, from either the west or south region, that has not been cancelled. You combine several of the techniques above into one filter.

code.content:
target_orders = df[
    (df["total"] > 500)
    & (df["region"].isin(["west", "south"]))
    & (~df["status"].isin(["cancelled"]))
]

# or, more readable with query
target_orders = df.query(
    "total > 500 and region in ['west', 'south'] and status != 'cancelled'"
)

blocks.alt: Narrowing an orders DataFrame down step by step through several combined conditions
blocks.caption: Each condition narrows the result further, ending with exactly the target rows.

blocks.text: 8. Recap

items: df[condition] filters rows using a boolean Series, the same idea as NumPy boolean masking.
Combine conditions with & and |, never Python's and/or, and always wrap each condition in parentheses.
.query() is often more readable for complex conditions and lets you use plain and/or.
.isin() checks membership against a list of values, and ~ negates any condition.
.str.contains() gives you a first taste of text based filtering, covered fully later.
